clinician.final_diagnosis: Pityriasis rubra pilaris (PRP) - generalized papulodescamative disease
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 32-month-old male presented with a 4-day history of progressive pruritic exanthem beginning on the hands and feet, spreading to the entire body including the face. Initial misdiagnosis as urticaria or staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome led to hospitalization and empiric oxacillin IV therapy (100 mg/kg/day every 6 hours). Physical examination on admission revealed generalized erythema, follicular papules, and progressive non-painful desquamative exanthem on hands, feet, genitalia, and periorificial areas. Dermatology evaluation on hospital day 7 documented diffuse erythematosquamous plaques with cephalocaudal evolution, follicular hyperkeratosis, palmoplantar keratoderma, and characteristic areas of healthy skin (islands of sparing). The patient was identified as post-infected with COVID-19 based on family epidemiological history. A clinical diagnosis of generalized papulodescamative disease compatible with pityriasis rubra pilaris was made, and alternative diagnoses (psoriasis, seborrheic dermatitis, erythrokeratoderma, follicular eczema, ichthyosis, frinoderma, and atypical keratosis pilaris) were ruled out. Oxacillin was discontinued, and treatment was changed to topical care (glycerin soap cleaning and rehydrating cream), cetirizine 0.5 mg/kg/day every 2 days, and prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day. The patient showed clinical improvement during hospitalization and was discharged. At 14-day follow-up, clinical improvement persisted with residual erythematous lesions on trunk and extremities. At 3-month follow-up, complete clinical resolution of dermatological lesions was documented.
